input:
This staffing review takes a detailed look at the position in a dispatch office that currently employs 8 full-time staff, and it considers whether an additional hire should be made in order to reduce the office's reliance on overtime. Over the course of last year, overtime stood at 6% of paid hours, and it is interesting to note that this overtime was not spread evenly across the year but was instead concentrated in 2 seasonal peaks. Replacing half of the overtime with 1 additional hire would cost $60k per year on a fully loaded basis, and it is this option that the review weighs up in what follows.

When the trade-off is examined more closely, a number of considerations come into view. The hire would cost $60k for the full year in order to remove 3% of paid hours, which is to say half of the 6% overtime share, and those hours arise in 2 seasonal peaks rather than across the year as a whole. Outside the peaks, in other words, the additional hire would be paid for hours that the office does not really need to have covered.

Overtime, by contrast, is bought only in the weeks that actually need it, which is one of its principal attractions in this context. The current arrangement pays for cover in the 2 peaks and pays nothing towards cover in the rest of the year. At the same time, however, its weakness lies in concentration: it is the same 8 staff who carry the peaks, and a peak that grows, or a peak that happens to coincide with absence, falls on a fixed team with limited room for manoeuvre.

Taking all of this into account, the position that emerges is a fairly narrow one. Staffing stays at 8, overtime continues to carry the 2 peaks, and the case for 1 additional hire would be reopened only when the overtime share rises above 6% of paid hours or the overtime begins to spread outside the peaks. On the figures for last year, it has to be said that neither of those conditions is met.
target:
The dispatch office should keep its current staffing of 8 full-time staff and meet its seasonal peaks with overtime. The evidence base is last year's paid hours: overtime stood at 6% of paid hours, concentrated in 2 seasonal peaks. 1 additional hire, at $60k per year fully loaded, would replace half of that overtime, and the dispatch office manager should hold the hire until overtime spreads beyond the peaks.

The trade-off stands in one comparison. The hire costs $60k for the full year to remove 3% of paid hours (half of the 6% overtime share), and those hours arise in 2 seasonal peaks rather than across the year. Outside the peaks, the additional hire is paid for hours the office does not need covered.

The mismatch is one of timing. Overtime follows the work: it is available in the peak weeks and absent in the quiet weeks, at no standing cost. A hire reverses the pattern, at a standing cost in every week, quiet weeks included. The figures in this review fix the cost of the hire and the size and placing of the overtime, and the placing is the point.

Overtime, by contrast, is bought only in the weeks that need it. The current arrangement pays for cover in the 2 peaks and pays nothing towards cover in the rest of the year. Its weakness is concentration: the same 8 staff carry the peaks, and a peak that grows, or a peak that coincides with absence, falls on a fixed team.

The position to hold is therefore narrow. Staffing stays at 8, overtime continues to carry the 2 peaks, and the case for 1 additional hire is reopened only when the overtime share rises above 6% of paid hours or the overtime spreads outside the peaks. On last year's figures, neither condition is met.
